# Transit Mk6 Auxiliary Drive Belt Refit: A Diagnostic Checklist

Losing power steering and brake servo assistance simultaneously is a classic symptom of an auxiliary drive belt failure on the Ford Transit Mk6 (2003â2006). In your specific case, the absence of loud squealing prior to the incident suggests the belt didn't just slip; it likely jumped its tensioner or sheared off entirely once the system lost hydraulic pressure from the power steering pump. The brief faint squeal and subsequent hot rubber smell you noticed were early warnings that the belt had begun to ride on the edge of a pulley or that the tensioner was failing to maintain clamping force.

When refitting the serpentine belt, the goal is not just to loop it around the pulleys but to ensure the system operates within its designed geometric constraints. The image you provided shows the belt hanging off the lower-left pulley. This pulley appears smooth and non-ridged. On this model, the alternator (or water pump, depending on the specific configuration) often utilizes a smooth idler or drive pulley that relies on precise belt seating rather than flanges to keep the belt in place.

### Verifying Pulley Geometry and Tensioner Function

Before installing the new belt, inspect the tensioner assembly closely. You mentioned it was replaced two years ago, but rubber components degrade regardless of age. The most common failure mode is a worn bearing or a weak spring within the tensioner arm. If the tensioner arm cannot apply sufficient force to the belt, the system relies entirely on friction against smooth pulleys.

Check the tensioner pivot point for play. There should be no lateral movement in the arm when you press down on it manually. If there is slack, the new belt will likely ride up and off the pulley again within a few miles. Additionally, inspect the grooves (if present) or the face of every pulley. A belt that has jumped once often leaves micro-scratches or glazed spots on the pulley rim. While these might seem minor, they reduce the coefficient of friction needed to keep the belt seated on smooth surfaces.

### Routing and Seating Procedure

The Haynes manual is your primary reference here, but execution matters more than reading instructions. The Transit Mk6 belt routing can be tricky because the belt must pass behind certain tensioners before being clamped down. Do not simply pull the belt into place with a hammer or excessive force, as this can twist the belt or damage the harmonic balancer teeth if your engine uses one (though the 2.4L usually employs V-belts or specific serpentine profiles).

Once the belt is routed correctly and the tensioner is depressed to hold it open, use the tool provided in the kitâor a long breaker bar with the correct socketâto lock the tensioner down while you fully seat the belt on every pulley. This step is critical for smooth pulleys. You must ensure the belt sits flat against the entire circumference of the rim before releasing the tensioner. If you release it while the belt is slightly lifted, gravity and centrifugal force will pull it back off immediately upon engine start.

### Thermal Expansion Considerations

You noted a hot rubber smell earlier. This indicates the belt was running at high temperature before failing. Rubber expands when hot and contracts when cold. If you refit the belt when the engine and components are still warm, you might be setting up a false sense of security. A belt that fits perfectly while hot may become too loose once it cools down, leading to rapid re-failure. Ideally, allow the engine block and alternator housing to cool completely before attempting the installation. This ensures the pulleys have contracted slightly, giving you a clearer view of any misalignment or damage that might only be visible at ambient temperatures.

### Final Inspection Before Starting

Before cranking the engine, spin each pulley by hand. They should rotate freely without grinding or binding. Listen for any clicking sounds that indicate a failing bearing in the alternator, idler, or tensioner. If you find noise now, replacing the belt is futile; you will destroy the new belt before it leaves the shop.

If the belt remains seated after a short test run and no further power steering assist is lost, the issue was likely mechanical fatigue of the old belt combined with a marginal tensioner that finally gave up under thermal stress. Monitor the belt for the first few hundred miles; if you notice rapid glazing or slipping, revisit the tensioner bearing check immediately.
